newsitem.title: BELGIUM: INTERVIEW-Partial EU tax harmony unwise - EU's Monti.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Partial EU tax harmony unwise - EU's Monti.

text.p: European Commissioner Mario Monti said on Monday that it was wishful thinking to believe that some European Union states could move towards common taxes ahead of the others.

Monti, who is responsible for the EU's Internal Market, told Reuters he did not believe that flexibility -- the current "in" word in Brussels meaning greater European integration by groups of nations rather than the whole bloc -- could apply to tax.
"The aplication of flexibility to taxation would be unwise, self-defeating and inappropriate," he said in an interview, adding that this should be envisaged only as "a last resort".

It was highly inappropriate to divide the EU into tax groups, Monti said, arguing that taxation was at the very core of the European single market for people, goods, services and capital which was created in 1993.
Monti's main brief is to ensure that the market of 370 million people works properly.
It was unlikely a group of EU countries would go ahead, for example, with a common tax on income from capital because they would be at a disadvantage to partners not imposing such a tax.
"The member states not participating in reinforced cooperation will hold back the others from making progresss in tax coordination," Monti said.

The debate on the possibility a limited group of countries could press ahead with single tax plans raged across Europe last week as several EU countries and the European Commission put forward ideas on the future workings of the 15-nation bloc.
The debate is part of efforts to adapt EU institutions to the expected enlargement of the Union to eastern Europe.

France and Germany, the driving force within the Union, are also reported to favour closer tax integration under Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), due to enter its final stage with a single currency at the end of 1999.
Monti, echoing the view of Commission President Jacques Santer, said EMU did not involve any additional requirements regarding taxation.

But others see taxation as a prime target for more ambitious integration moves, given the lack of progress on standardising national Value Added Tax levels, corporate tax and tax on dividends and other capital gains. This is because tax issues require the unanimous vote of EU ministers.
The Commission suggested at the inter-governmental conference on reforming the EU that majority voting should be extended to avoid one country being able to block plans indefinitely.
Luxembourg, for example, has so far prevented a deal on taxing income from capital, arguing that this should be agreed at the wider level of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Luxembourg, which is under pressure from higher-tax neighbours Germany and Belgium, is worried that if it agrees to the plan, savings currently invested in its financial sector will flow to more favourable places outside the EU.
Monti thought progress on a capital income tax was possible EU-wide if the debate also addressed the question of the numerous European "tax havens".
